title: Definition of a hydrocarbon
statement: define the term hydrocarbon as a compound made up of $\ce{C}$ and $\ce{H}$ atoms only

title: Alkanes as hydrocarbons without functional groups
statement: understand that alkanes are simple hydrocarbons with no functional group

title: Functional groups determine properties
statement: understand that the compounds in the table on pages 29 and 30 contain a functional group which dictates their physical and chemical properties

title: General, structural, displayed and skeletal formulas
statement: interpret and use the general, structural, displayed and skeletal formulas of the classes of compound stated in the table on pages 29 and 30

title: IUPAC nomenclature of organic molecules
statement: understand and use systematic nomenclature of simple aliphatic organic molecules with functional groups detailed in the table on pages 29 and 30, up to six carbon atoms (six plus six for esters, straight chains only for esters and nitriles)

title: Deducing molecular and empirical formula
statement: deduce the molecular and/or empirical formula of a compound, given its structural, displayed or skeletal formula

title: Key organic chemistry terminology
statement: interpret and use the following terminology associated with types of organic compounds and reactions: (a) homologous series (b) saturated and unsaturated (c) homolytic and heterolytic fission (d) free radical, initiation, propagation, termination (e) nucleophile, electrophile, nucleophilic, electrophilic (f) addition, substitution, elimination, hydrolysis, condensation (g) oxidation and reduction (in equations for organic redox reactions, the symbol [O] can be used to represent one atom of oxygen from an oxidising agent and the symbol [H] to represent one atom of hydrogen from a reducing agent)

title: Types of organic reaction mechanisms
statement: understand and use the following terminology associated with types of organic mechanisms: (a) free-radical substitution (b) electrophilic addition (c) nucleophilic substitution (d) nucleophilic addition (in organic reaction mechanisms, the use of curly arrows to represent movement of electron pairs is expected; the arrow should begin at a bond or a lone pair of electrons)

title: Straight-chain, branched and cyclic molecules
statement: describe organic molecules as either straight-chained, branched or cyclic

title: Shapes from sp, sp2 and sp3 hybridisation
statement: describe and explain the shape of, and bond angles in, molecules containing $sp$, $sp^2$ and $sp^3$ hybridised atoms

title: Sigma and pi bonds in hybridised atoms
statement: describe the arrangement of σ and π bonds in molecules containing $sp$, $sp^2$ and $sp^3$ hybridised atoms

title: Planar arrangement in organic molecules
statement: understand and use the term planar when describing the arrangement of atoms in organic molecules, for example ethene

title: Types of structural isomerism
statement: describe structural isomerism and its division into chain, positional and functional group isomerism

title: Types of stereoisomerism
statement: describe stereoisomerism and its division into geometrical (cis/trans) and optical isomerism (use of E/Z nomenclature is acceptable but is not required)

title: Cis-trans isomerism in alkenes
statement: describe geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism in alkenes, and explain its origin in terms of restricted rotation due to the presence of π bonds

title: Chiral centres and enantiomers
statement: explain what is meant by a chiral centre and that such a centre gives rise to two optical isomers (enantiomers) (Candidates should appreciate that compounds can contain more than one chiral centre, but knowledge of meso compounds, or nomenclature such as diastereoisomers is not required.)

title: Identifying chiral and geometrical isomerism
statement: identify chiral centres and geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism in a molecule of given structural formula including cyclic compounds

title: Deducing isomers from molecular formula
statement: deduce the possible isomers for an organic molecule of known molecular formula

title: Preparing alkanes: hydrogenation and cracking
statement: recall the reactions (reagents and conditions) by which alkanes can be produced: (a) addition of hydrogen to an alkene in a hydrogenation reaction, $\ce{H2(g)}$ and Pt/Ni catalyst and heat (b) cracking of a longer chain alkane, heat with $\ce{Al2O3}$

title: Combustion and substitution reactions of alkanes
statement: describe: (a) the complete and incomplete combustion of alkanes (b) the free-radical substitution of alkanes by $\ce{Cl2}$ or $\ce{Br2}$ in the presence of ultraviolet light, as exemplified by the reactions of ethane

title: Free-radical substitution mechanism
statement: describe the mechanism of free-radical substitution with reference to the initiation, propagation and termination steps

title: Cracking crude oil fractions
statement: suggest how cracking can be used to obtain more useful alkanes and alkenes of lower $M_r$ from heavier crude oil fractions

title: Unreactivity of alkanes
statement: understand the general unreactivity of alkanes, including towards polar reagents in terms of the strength of the $\ce{C-H}$ bonds and their relative lack of polarity

title: Environmental impact of alkane combustion
statement: recognise the environmental consequences of carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and unburnt hydrocarbons arising from the combustion of alkanes in the internal combustion engine and of their catalytic removal

title: Preparing alkenes: elimination and dehydration
statement: recall the reactions (including reagents and conditions) by which alkenes can be produced: (a) elimination of $\ce{HX}$ from a halogenoalkane by ethanolic $\ce{NaOH}$ and heat (b) dehydration of an alcohol, by using a heated catalyst (e.g. $\ce{Al2O3}$) or a concentrated acid (e.g. concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$) (c) cracking of a longer chain alkane

title: Electrophilic addition and oxidation of alkenes
statement: describe the following reactions of alkenes: (a) the electrophilic addition of (i) hydrogen in a hydrogenation reaction, $\ce{H2(g)}$ and Pt/Ni catalyst and heat (ii) steam, $\ce{H2O(g)}$ and $\ce{H3PO4}$ catalyst (iii) a hydrogen halide, $\ce{HX(g)}$, at room temperature (iv) a halogen, $\ce{X2}$ (b) the oxidation by cold dilute acidified $\ce{KMnO4}$ to form the diol (c) the oxidation by hot concentrated acidified $\ce{KMnO4}$ leading to the rupture of the carbon-carbon double bond and the identities of the subsequent products to determine the position of alkene linkages in larger molecules (d) addition polymerisation exemplified by the reactions of ethene and propene

title: Bromine water test for C=C bonds
statement: describe the use of aqueous bromine to show the presence of a $\ce{C=C}$ bond

title: Mechanism of electrophilic addition
statement: describe the mechanism of electrophilic addition in alkenes, using bromine/ethene and hydrogen bromide/propene as examples

title: Inductive effects and Markovnikov addition
statement: describe and explain the inductive effects of alkyl groups on the stability of primary, secondary and tertiary cations formed during electrophilic addition (this should be used to explain Markovnikov addition)

title: Preparing halogenoalkanes
statement: recall the reactions (reagents and conditions) by which halogenoalkanes can be produced: (a) the free-radical substitution of alkanes by $\ce{Cl2}$ or $\ce{Br2}$ in the presence of ultraviolet light, as exemplified by the reactions of ethane (b) electrophilic addition of an alkene with a halogen, $\ce{X2}$, or hydrogen halide, $\ce{HX(g)}$, at room temperature (c) substitution of an alcohol, e.g. by reaction with $\ce{HX(g)}$; or with $\ce{KCl}$ and concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$ or concentrated $\ce{H3PO4}$; or with $\ce{PCl3}$ and heat; or with $\ce{PCl5}$; or with $\ce{SOCl2}$

title: Classifying halogenoalkanes
statement: classify halogenoalkanes into primary, secondary and tertiary

title: Nucleophilic substitution of halogenoalkanes
statement: describe the following nucleophilic substitution reactions: (a) the reaction with $\ce{NaOH(aq)}$ and heat to produce an alcohol (b) the reaction with $\ce{KCN}$ in ethanol and heat to produce a nitrile (c) the reaction with $\ce{NH3}$ in ethanol heated under pressure to produce an amine (d) the reaction with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol as a method of identifying the halogen present as exemplified by bromoethane

title: Elimination reaction of halogenoalkanes
statement: describe the elimination reaction with $\ce{NaOH}$ in ethanol and heat to produce an alkene as exemplified by bromoethane

title: SN1 and SN2 mechanisms
statement: describe the $S_N1$ and $S_N2$ mechanisms of nucleophilic substitution in halogenoalkanes including the inductive effects of alkyl groups

title: SN1/SN2 preference by halogenoalkane class
statement: recall that primary halogenoalkanes tend to react via the $S_N2$ mechanism; tertiary halogenoalkanes via the $S_N1$ mechanism; and secondary halogenoalkanes by a mixture of the two, depending on structure

title: Reactivity trends of halogenoalkanes
statement: describe and explain the different reactivities of halogenoalkanes (with particular reference to the relative strengths of the $\ce{C-X}$ bonds as exemplified by the reactions of halogenoalkanes with aqueous silver nitrates)

title: Preparing alcohols
statement: recall the reactions (reagents and conditions) by which alcohols can be produced: (a) electrophilic addition of steam to an alkene, $\ce{H2O(g)}$ and $\ce{H3PO4}$ catalyst (b) reaction of alkenes with cold dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII) to form a diol (c) substitution of a halogenoalkane using $\ce{NaOH(aq)}$ and heat (d) reduction of an aldehyde or ketone using $\ce{NaBH4}$ or $\ce{LiAlH4}$ (e) reduction of a carboxylic acid using $\ce{LiAlH4}$ (f) hydrolysis of an ester using dilute acid or dilute alkali and heat

title: Reactions of alcohols
statement: describe: (a) the reaction with oxygen (combustion) (b) substitution to form halogenoalkanes, e.g. by reaction with $\ce{HX(g)}$; or with $\ce{KCl}$ and concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$ or concentrated $\ce{H3PO4}$; or with $\ce{PCl3}$ and heat; or with $\ce{PCl5}$; or with $\ce{SOCl2}$ (c) the reaction with $\ce{Na(s)}$ (d) oxidation with acidified $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ or acidified $\ce{KMnO4}$ to: (i) carbonyl compounds by distillation (ii) carboxylic acids by refluxing (primary alcohols give aldehydes which can be further oxidised to carboxylic acids, secondary alcohols give ketones, tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidised) (e) dehydration to an alkene, by using a heated catalyst, e.g. $\ce{Al2O3}$ or a concentrated acid (f) formation of esters by reaction with carboxylic acids and concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$ as catalyst as exemplified by ethanol

title: Classifying and distinguishing alcohols
statement: (a) classify alcohols as primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, to include examples with more than one alcohol group (b) state characteristic distinguishing reactions, e.g. mild oxidation with acidified $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$, colour change from orange to green

title: Iodoform test for alcohols
statement: deduce the presence of a $\ce{CH3CH(OH)-}$ group in an alcohol, $\ce{CH3CH(OH)-R}$, from its reaction with alkaline $\ce{I2(aq)}$ to form a yellow precipitate of tri-iodomethane and an ion, $\ce{RCO2^-}$

title: Acidity of alcohols vs water
statement: explain the acidity of alcohols compared with water

title: Preparing aldehydes and ketones
statement: recall the reactions (reagents and conditions) by which aldehydes and ketones can be produced: (a) the oxidation of primary alcohols using acidified $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ or acidified $\ce{KMnO4}$ and distillation to produce aldehydes (b) the oxidation of secondary alcohols using acidified $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ or acidified $\ce{KMnO4}$ and distillation to produce ketones

title: Reduction and HCN addition to carbonyls
statement: describe: (a) the reduction of aldehydes and ketones using $\ce{NaBH4}$ or $\ce{LiAlH4}$ to produce alcohols (b) the reaction of aldehydes and ketones with $\ce{HCN}$, $\ce{KCN}$ as catalyst, and heat to produce hydroxynitriles as exemplified by ethanal and propanone

title: Nucleophilic addition mechanism with HCN
statement: describe the mechanism of the nucleophilic addition reactions of hydrogen cyanide with aldehydes and ketones in 17.1.2(b)

title: 2,4-DNPH test for carbonyls
statement: describe the use of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH reagent) to detect the presence of carbonyl compounds

title: Distinguishing aldehydes from ketones
statement: deduce the nature (aldehyde or ketone) of an unknown carbonyl compound from the results of simple tests (Fehling’s and Tollens’ reagents; ease of oxidation)

title: Iodoform test for methyl carbonyls
statement: deduce the presence of a $\ce{CH3CO-}$ group in an aldehyde or ketone, $\ce{CH3CO-R}$, from its reaction with alkaline $\ce{I2(aq)}$ to form a yellow precipitate of tri-iodomethane and an ion, $\ce{RCO2^-}$

title: Preparing carboxylic acids
statement: recall the reactions by which carboxylic acids can be produced: (a) oxidation of primary alcohols and aldehydes with acidified $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ or acidified $\ce{KMnO4}$ and refluxing (b) hydrolysis of nitriles with dilute acid or dilute alkali followed by acidification (c) hydrolysis of esters with dilute acid or dilute alkali and heat followed by acidification

title: Reactions of carboxylic acids
statement: describe: (a) the redox reaction with reactive metals to produce a salt and $\ce{H2(g)}$ (b) the neutralisation reaction with alkalis to produce a salt and $\ce{H2O(l)}$ (c) the acid–base reaction with carbonates to produce a salt and $\ce{H2O(l)}$ and $\ce{CO2(g)}$ (d) esterification with alcohols with concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$ as catalyst (e) reduction by $\ce{LiAlH4}$ to form a primary alcohol

title: Preparing esters by esterification
statement: recall the reaction (reagents and conditions) by which esters can be produced: (a) the condensation reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid with concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$ as catalyst

title: Hydrolysis of esters
statement: describe the hydrolysis of esters by dilute acid and by dilute alkali and heat

title: Preparing primary amines
statement: recall the reactions by which amines can be produced: (a) reaction of a halogenoalkane with $\ce{NH3}$ in ethanol heated under pressure (Classification of amines will not be tested at AS Level.)

title: Preparing nitriles
statement: recall the reactions by which nitriles can be produced: (a) reaction of a halogenoalkane with $\ce{KCN}$ in ethanol and heat

title: Preparing hydroxynitriles
statement: recall the reactions by which hydroxynitriles can be produced: (a) the reaction of aldehydes and ketones with $\ce{HCN}$, $\ce{KCN}$ as catalyst, and heat

title: Hydrolysis of nitriles
statement: describe the hydrolysis of nitriles with dilute acid or dilute alkali followed by acidification to produce a carboxylic acid

title: Addition polymerisation
statement: describe addition polymerisation as exemplified by poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene), PVC

title: Deducing polymer repeat units
statement: deduce the repeat unit of an addition polymer obtained from a given monomer

title: Identifying monomers from polymer structure
statement: identify the monomer(s) present in a given section of an addition polymer molecule

title: Environmental impact of poly(alkene) disposal
statement: recognise the difficulty of the disposal of poly(alkene)s, i.e. non-biodegradability and harmful combustion products

title: Identifying functional groups and predicting reactions
statement: for an organic molecule containing several functional groups: (a) identify organic functional groups using the reactions in the syllabus (b) predict properties and reactions

title: Devising multi-step synthetic routes
statement: devise multi-step synthetic routes for preparing organic molecules using the reactions in the syllabus

title: Analysing synthetic routes
statement: analyse a given synthetic route in terms of type of reaction and reagents used for each step of it, and possible by-products

title: Interpreting infrared spectra
statement: analyse an infrared spectrum of a simple molecule to identify functional groups (see the Data section for the functional groups required)

title: Interpreting mass spectra
statement: analyse mass spectra in terms of $m/e$ values and isotopic abundances (knowledge of the working of the mass spectrometer is not required)

title: Calculating relative atomic mass from isotopes
statement: calculate the relative atomic mass of an element given the relative abundances of its isotopes, or its mass spectrum

title: Molecular ion peak and molecular mass
statement: deduce the molecular mass of an organic molecule from the molecular ion peak in a mass spectrum

title: Fragmentation patterns in mass spectra
statement: suggest the identity of molecules formed by simple fragmentation in a given mass spectrum

title: Carbon count from M+1 peak
statement: deduce the number of carbon atoms, $n$, in a compound using the $[M+1]^+$ peak and the formula $n = \dfrac{100 \times \text{abundance of } [M+1]^+ \text{ ion}}{1.1 \times \text{abundance of } M^+ \text{ ion}}$

title: Bromine and chlorine from M+2 peak
statement: deduce the presence of bromine and chlorine atoms in a compound using the $[M+2]^+$ peak
